gap: No result ChatGPT got states how tall the travel tripods are with the centre column down. On the maker or reviewer spec sheets, the Ulanzi Zero Y drops from 156.7 to 132.7 cm, the Peak Design Travel Tripod from 152.4 to 130.2 cm and the Manfrotto Befree Advanced lever kit from 151 to 128 cm, so the steady-in-wind heights sit within 4.7 cm of each other.
standout_why: I compared against three cited pages. digitalnomads.world (cited in chat 1) gives Peak Design aluminium 152.4 cm and Ulanzi Zero Y 156.7 cm without saying whether the centre column is up. It does split the Zero Y load ratings (3 kg head, 5 kg, 18 kg column), so that part is not new. findingtheuniverse.com (cited in chat 2) tells readers to check the height with the column down and says about 60 in reaches eye level. It gives no column-down figure for any tripod, and its Befree is the GT XPRO, not the Advanced. It also does not say that only Manfrotto rates its payload to a published standard. amateurphotographer.com (cited in both chats) returned HTTP 403, so I could not check it.
decides: This confirms the order but shrinks the gap. With the column down, the Zero Y is still tallest (132.7 cm), then Peak Design (130.2 cm), then the Befree Advanced (128 cm). The 5.7 cm headline spread drops to 4.7 cm. All three land about 51–52 in, roughly 8–9 in below the 60 in eye level that findingtheuniverse cites, so a buyer wanting eye level without the column should look at a taller kit like the Sirui 7C (166.5 cm headline). The load figures differ too. Manfrotto's 9 kg is the only one rated to a stated standard (UNI/PdR 105:2021). Peak Design's 9.1 kg comes without a test method. The Zero Y's head is the limit: its spec list says 3 kg and its overview says 5 kg. So for heavy lenses, the Befree and the Peak Design rank ahead of the Zero Y, even though the Zero Y headlines an 18 kg column figure.
